title: Maha Shivaratri: the great night of Shiva
hook: a night kept awake, water poured over the lingam, Om Namah Shivaya until dawn
tomorrow: Raksha Bandhan: the thread of protection

segments.voice: Yesterday: Holi in Braj, Krishna's colors, sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan. Your line was everyone's the same color today. Did you find something in common with someone? Day six hundred eighty-two.

Look closely at many images of Shiva and you'll notice his throat is a darker blue than the rest of him. It isn't a painting mistake. It's a scar, of a kind. One of his names is Nilakantha, the blue-throated. And one of the stories people tell about Maha Shivaratri is the story of how his throat got that color: a moment when the whole universe nearly ended, and one god drank the danger so everyone else could live.
screen: `A BLUE THROAT.` → `NILAKANTHA.` → `THE NIGHT HE DRANK THE DANGER.`

segments.voice: The Bhagavata Purana tells it in its eighth book. The gods and the demons, usually enemies, agree to work together for once. They want amrita, the nectar of immortality, and it lies at the bottom of the ocean of milk. So they churn the ocean. They use a mountain, Mandara, as the churning stick, and the great serpent Vasuki as the rope, gods pulling one end, demons the other. This is the samudra manthan, the churning of the ocean. But the first thing that rises from the churning isn't nectar. It's poison. Halahala, a poison so strong its fumes spread in every direction and begin to burn the worlds. Gods, demons, every creature, run. And they run to Shiva. The text says Shiva looks on them with compassion, and his wife, the Goddess, agrees. He gathers the poison in his palm and drinks it. And then, in the telling many know, he holds it in his throat. He doesn't swallow it all the way down, where it would destroy him and the world inside him, and he doesn't spit it out, where it would destroy everyone else. He keeps it right there, and his throat turns blue. Some devotees connect Shivaratri to that night: that the gods stayed awake, singing to Shiva, so the poison wouldn't overcome him. It's one explanation among several. But it fits the vigil. The night isn't only about staying up. It's about keeping someone company while they hold something hard.
screen: `THE CHURNING OF THE OCEAN.` · `FIRST, NOT NECTAR, BUT POISON.` · `SHIVA DRINKS IT.` · `HELD IN THE THROAT: NILAKANTHA.` · then, large: `KEEP COMPANY WITH THE ONE WHO HOLDS IT.`

segments.voice: Sit upright and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you're holding right now that you can't swallow and can't spit out: a worry, a hard conversation coming, a grief. Don't push it down, and don't push it away. Just let it sit in the throat or the chest while you breathe around it. Keep it company, the way the gods kept Shiva company. The bell holds the time.
Shivaratri. The great night of Shiva, the blue-throated one, who held the world's poison so others could live.
Your line: stay awake for what matters. Today, stay with someone who's holding something hard, even just with a message that says you're there. Day six hundred eighty-two.

howItsDone: On Maha Shivaratri many Hindus keep vigil at Shiva temples through the night, chanting and offering water, milk and bilva leaves to the lingam; some connect the night with Shiva drinking the poison from the churned ocean.

pairs: the mountain used as the churning stick
the serpent used as the rope

myth: the first thing to rise from the churned ocean is the nectar
the poison halahala rises first, and begins to burn the worlds.
gods and demons pull together on the serpent rope
for once, they work together, one at each end.
in a well-known telling, Shiva holds the poison in his throat
neither swallowing nor spitting it out, so his throat turns blue.

fork.setup: you're Shiva. a poison is burning the worlds, and every creature runs to you. what do you do?
options: drink the poison and hold it in your throat.
fork.reveal: out of compassion, and with the Goddess agreeing, he drinks it. held in his throat, it turns it blue.

original.note: Sanskrit nīla (blue) + kaṇṭha (throat): Shiva, the blue-throated.

trapdoor: what you thought: Shiva's blue throat is just how he's painted.
what it means: it's the mark of the poison he held to save the worlds.
what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata Purana's eighth book tells Shiva drinking the halahala at the churning of the ocean; the link to Shivaratri's vigil is one of several explanations people give.

sources.ref: Bhagavata Purana 8.7 (the churning of the ocean; Shiva drinks the halahala)

notes: Confirm Bhagavata 8.7 details: Shiva's compassion, the Goddess (Bhavani) consenting, the poison taken in the palm and drunk, the throat turning blue.
'Holding it in the throat' (neither swallowed nor spat out) is the common telling; in some tellings Parvati presses his throat to stop it. Confirm phrasing.
Reviewer: hook changed from 'swallowed' to 'drank' so it doesn't contradict the teach (held in the throat, not swallowed).
The link between the vigil and the gods keeping Shiva awake is a popular explanation; marked as one among several.

Editor review: removed 'the most common telling' (unsourced superlative); the churning is no longer called a night (the Bhagavata does not say so); practice ending changed so it doesn't repeat day 675's 'three more breaths'.
